title: Karmic tail 15 20 5 in the destiny matrix: when a rule and a craving add up to a trial of yourself

seo.title: 15 20 5 in the destiny matrix: karmic tail M–N–D
seo.description: Tail 15-20-5 in the destiny matrix: The Devil, Judgement and The Hierophant in the strict order M–N–D, the formula and a practical reading.

short: If your karmic tail is 15-20-5, at its base there is no curse but a collision of two forces: the rule of “how it should be” absorbed in childhood (5 The Hierophant) and a living bodily desire that does not fit inside that rule (15 The Devil). Where they meet, the inner judge switches on — 20 Judgement, and the whole triple describes one script: the rule puts the desire on trial, hands down the verdict “I am wrong”, the person holds the rule tighter still — and the desire pushes harder. It all turns on the point of judgement, and the way out is there too.

sections.h2: The rule of “how it should be” and the hunger that will not fit into it
paragraphs: At the root of the triple stands 5 The Hierophant — but here he is not a wise teacher in general, he is one specific absorbed rule: the family formula that says “the right way to live is like this”, “you must not want that”, “earn it first”. The rule was taken on trust from an authority — parents, the people around you, tradition — and is held as the truth rather than as one version of it. Next to it, in the manifestation, stands 15 The Devil: a living bodily pull towards whatever really attracts you, be it money, another person, pleasure or power. The pull does not reason and does not ask permission — it simply pulls.

On their own neither of these arcana creates a problem: the rule gives support, the desire gives force. The tail is born at the joint between them. An absorbed “must not” and a living “I want” point in different directions and never meet on good terms — tension collects between them, and there is more of it each time round. A karmic tail here is a repeating script inherited through the family line: rule and desire collide again and again until a person takes the mechanism apart, instead of simply suppressing one side with the other once more.

sections.h2: Why 5 and 15 add up to Judgement in particular
paragraphs: The middle arcanum N is not random: the formula adds the outer positions M and D. Here 15 The Devil plus 5 The Hierophant give 20 Judgement. The addition does not change the order 15-20-5: the desire is at the entry, the rule is at the root, and Judgement between them becomes the mechanism of an inner hearing. When “I must” and “I want” pull in different directions, it is Judgement that asks again: “how are you living with this?”.

Judgement is the energy of the summing-up and of an inner judge who sits without days off. It raises everything that has collected between the rule and the desire and presents it all at once: do you match the absorbed “how it should be”, or once again you do not. And this is where the triple either breaks open or closes into a circle — everything depends on what the verdict turns out to be. A strong Judgement honestly reviews whether the old rule still fits. A weak one sentences whoever dared to want.

sections.h2: How the judge turns desire into guilt and starts another turn
paragraphs: In the weak version of the twentieth arcanum the judge works against the person. Faced with a pull that the rule forbids, it does not ask where the rule came from or whether it is still alive — it appoints a guilty party straight away, and the guilty party is always the desire. The sentence sounds like “I am wrong”, “I am weak”, “there is something off about me”. Notice the substitution: what goes on trial is not the outdated “must not”, but the plain fact that a person wants something. The Hierophant even supplies a ready wording for the guilt — in the language of that same inherited norm.

A sentence like that does not set anyone free; it drives them round another turn. If “I am weak”, then the rule has to be kept more strictly — and the person goes back to The Hierophant and tightens the “must not”. But the harder a desire is pressed down, the more insistently it breaks out: The Devil cannot stand a ban or a half-measure, and under pressure he only gets hotter. The next collision comes out sharper, which means the next Judgement is harsher. That is how the triple turns itself: the rule breeds guilt, guilt strengthens the rule, the tightened rule inflames the desire — and back to the dock again.

sections.h2: Being right as an addiction of its own: an unexpected turn
paragraphs: This triple has a second, less obvious form. Sometimes The Devil — the object of the addiction — is not a forbidden pleasure but the rule itself. Being the one who knows “how it is done properly”, holding the position of the elder who is always right, is a pull too, and it can hook you no worse than any substance. Then 15 latches not onto money or passion but onto the sweetness of one’s own rightness, while 5 gives that addiction the respectable shape of “principles”. Judgement in this version tries other people rather than the self — from above, in the name of a norm the person mistakes for the truth.

In life the triple surfaces in different ways. For one person it is a permanent sense of guilt over ordinary wishes and a swing of “gave in, repented, banned myself even more strictly”. For another it is harshness towards the people closest to them, measured against an absorbed code and constantly found guilty. For a third it is paralysed decisions: every “I want” first goes through a hearing on “am I even allowed”, and it never gets as far as the action. Different-looking stories, one root: desire meets a tribunal instead of a choice.

sections.h2: Where it breaks open: retry the rule, not the desire
paragraphs: The triple has one way out, and it lies at the point of judgement. While the verdict falls on the desire, the turn goes on. It breaks open at the moment the judge turns round and starts reviewing the rule itself: not “is my wanting right”, but “is this ‘must not’ still right, where did it come from, and have I ever tested it against my own experience”. That way the middle Judgement rethinks what was absorbed instead of executing what is alive. Three habits aim straight at the joint between these arcana rather than at each one separately.

Retry the norm, not yourself. When “I am wrong” rolls over you, that is the signal to turn the trial towards the rule: whose “must” is this, who passed it down and when, does it work in your life now. The Hierophant in his strong version does not defend the form, he keeps the meaning open — he doubts and he checks. A rule your own experience has not confirmed is a family hypothesis, not a sentence passed on you.

Call a desire a fact, not a sin. A pull is data about you, not evidence against you. “I want this” and “I am not allowed to want this” are different statements: the first can be looked at calmly, the second only drives you round the circle. A desire that has been acknowledged stops being The Devil as your master and becomes what it should be — fuel that you dispose of yourself.

Separate your own conclusion from the inherited one. The weak spot of the five is confusing being right with the truth and hiding behind authority. It helps to sort things literally: which parts of “how it should be” you have checked and are keeping, and which are simply “that is how it is done in our family”, held up by volume rather than sense. Whatever survived your check is yours; the rest can be let go without guilt.

faq.q: 15-20-5 and 5-20-15 — one tail or two different ones?
faq.a: Two different sequences. The page here reads only 15-20-5: 15 The Devil takes the entry position M, 20 Judgement the holding position N, and 5 The Hierophant the root position D. Rearranging them changes the roles and cannot pass as another spelling of the same tail.

faq.q: Is it true that arcanum 15 The Devil in a tail is about addiction and curses?
faq.a: About addiction, yes; about curses, no. In this triple The Devil means no magical influence but a living pull: towards a person, money, pleasure, or even towards your own rightness. The problem is not that the desire exists, it is that an absorbed rule tries it as guilt. Once mastered, that same force becomes fuel and the knack of seeing straight through people’s motives.

faq.q: What is the first thing to do with the 15-20-5 tail?
faq.a: Catch one moment — the point where an ordinary “I want” is followed inside by a hearing on “am I allowed to”. That is where the rule and the desire collide, and that is where guilt is born. The first step is not to ban the desire or to lean on the rule, but to turn the question round: not “is my wanting right”, but “is the rule itself still right”.

It is one of those the niche loves to dramatise — because of The Devil and a stern Judgement. But the weight here is not in a cruel fate, it is in the closed circle: rule and desire keep hitting each other while the judge executes instead of reviewing. The script has a clear exit point — retry the outdated “must not”. Lived through, this set gives a rare mixture: meaning, the force of desire and an honest inner account.
